editorial.summary: After an opening conversation about a private participant trying to conceive, David Choe, Asa Akira, Valentin, Money Mark and Steve Lee introduce the show. Asa reports her book entering a second printing and describes audiobook work; David returns from Hawaii and uses airport inconvenience, wealth and a confused argument about millennials to examine his habit of escaping difficulty. He says a major television project collapsed because the network found him too extreme, leaving him time for an intensive Hawaii therapy retreat. The podcast calls itself therapy, but the cast also calls it the Enablers Club and acknowledges that it replaced licensed treatment while encouraging dangerous ideas. David invites his aging parents, Critter, Harry Kim, a Mexico City partner, a former lover and another recurring woman in succession, then admits that every visit prevented the solitude he claimed to seek. A debate about whether pornography and DVDASA help anyone is unusually self-critical: entertainment and listener connection are weighed against damaged relationships, employment consequences, family strain and the podcast's cost to Asa. David connects service, creative maturation and thinking about another person to a hoped-for exit from arrested development. The title story begins when a private woman messages him after seeing him at a Kona restaurant. They talk for hours and rapidly build an intense relationship before meeting. Her prior-partner stories, private social media and apparent alignment with David's checklist make her seem both ideal and suspicious. A misunderstanding turns 'baby sister' and 'two mortgages' into an imagined child; David uses stigmatizing disability and body language while calling his willingness to raise that nonexistent child a breakthrough. When she panics and asks for time, he insists on an immediate public meeting, waits for eight hours, threatens to remain until he starves or dies, returns after being told the parking lot is closed and sends a confrontation video. Her brother reports a panic attack. The editorial record treats those actions as coercive pressure, not romance. David and the cast then speculate about catfishing, sex, gender and sociopathy, while his therapist reportedly reframes the attachment as evidence he can feel again. David declares the unseen woman his girlfriend and says he is in love; Part One ends without proving her identity, mutual relationship status or whether they ever meet. Every idea and offensive term remains as source evidence, while the private woman's name, business, family, phone, accounts, exact locations and health trail remain undiscoverable. Ten empty zero-duration records are the only cleaner drops, and no line receives a published speaker name.
